```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%", raster3d = 1e5, dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

An in-space view follows light rays from an observer inside a geometry.
The ray-marching backend supports the eight homogeneous three-dimensional
geometries studied by Thurston. This article renders an intrinsic scene in
each space, following the construction of Coulon, Matsumoto, Segerman and
Trettel [2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.15801). Installation is covered in
[Get started](ggplot3d.html).

## Positioning objects from the observer

A geodesic is the path followed by a freely travelling ray in a geometry.
Place three balls by travelling along three initial directions from the
origin. Their centres are at intrinsic distances of 1.5, 1.9 and 2.2 units,
and their radii are 0.22, 0.28 and 0.28. The same directions, distances and
radii are used in each scene, so changes in appearance come from the geometry.

```{r scene}
directions <- rbind(c(-0.4, -0.15, 1), c(0.3, 0.2, 1), c(0.1, -0.25, 1))
distances <- c(1.5, 1.9, 2.2)
radii <- c(0.22, 0.28, 0.28)
colours <- unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "green")])
inside <- function(geometry) {
  balls <- lapply(1:3, function(i) {
    centre <- geodesic_3d(geometry, direction = directions[i, ],
      distance = distances[i])$position
    geom_thurston_3d(center = as.numeric(centre), radius = radii[i],
      fill = colours[i])
  })
  ggplot() + balls + theme_void() +
    coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raymarch", geometry = geometry,
      dpi = 52, antialias = 1, max_distance = 3.5, max_steps = 256))
}
```

The initial observer is the origin and the view points along its positive
third frame direction. Intrinsic primitives use their geometry's chart
coordinates. Ordinary point, path and mesh layers are rejected by this
backend; use balls, cylinders, half-spaces or chart-defined traced SDFs.

## Euclidean space

Euclidean space has the familiar flat metric. Rays are straight and the
angular size of a small ball decreases with its distance. The three balls
provide a reference for the curved spaces below.

```{r e3, fig.alt="Observer view of three separated coloured balls in Euclidean space."}
inside("e3")
```

## Spherical space

Spherical three-space has positive curvature. Neighbouring rays can reconverge,
and geodesics return after a full circuit. Its stereographic chart represents
the space in three coordinates; the renderer follows the intrinsic rays
across the chart's pole. The more distant balls occupy larger angular regions
in this scene.

```{r s3, fig.alt="Three balls in spherical space, with enlarged angular extent for the distant balls."}
inside("s3")
```

## Hyperbolic space

Hyperbolic three-space has negative curvature. Neighbouring rays diverge,
which makes distant balls occupy smaller angles. Coordinates use the open
Poincare ball: every centre and observer must have Euclidean norm below one.
The geodesic positioning above supplies valid chart coordinates.

```{r h3, fig.alt="Three balls in hyperbolic space, with small angular extent for the distant balls."}
inside("h3")
```

## Spherical plane times a line

The product of a sphere and a Euclidean line curves the first two directions
and leaves the third direction flat. Rays can reconverge in the spherical
factor while separating along the line. This directional dependence changes
the apparent outlines of balls viewed obliquely to the line.

```{r s2xe, fig.alt="Three intrinsic balls in the product of a spherical plane and a line."}
inside("s2xe")
```

## Hyperbolic plane times a line

The product of a hyperbolic plane and a Euclidean line expands ray separations
in its curved factor. Its line direction remains flat. The first two chart
coordinates lie in the open Poincare disk, and the third records distance
along the line.

```{r h2xe, fig.alt="Three intrinsic balls in the product of a hyperbolic plane and a line."}
inside("h2xe")
```

## Nil

Nil couples horizontal movement to the vertical coordinate. A horizontal
loop can produce vertical displacement, and geodesics with a vertical
component curve in the horizontal directions. The chart uses ordinary
three-component coordinates with this coupled distance rule. Intrinsic balls
can have asymmetric apparent outlines away from the viewing axis.

```{r nil, fig.alt="Three intrinsic balls viewed from the origin in Nil geometry."}
inside("nil")
```

## Sol

Sol stretches one horizontal direction and contracts the other as height
changes. Rotating a viewing direction therefore changes how rays separate
and how a surface appears. The ball primitive here uses the approximate
level set described in section 11.5 of Coulon and colleagues, with horizontal
weights that vary exponentially with height. These shapes illustrate that
approximation; their level-set definition is approximate.

```{r sol, fig.alt="Three approximate ball primitives in Sol, with direction-dependent outlines."}
inside("sol")
```

## The universal cover of SL(2, R)

This geometry combines a hyperbolic base with an unwrapped fibre direction.
The fibre records a continuously accumulated rotation; travelling around the
base changes that rotation. The chart uses two hyperboloid coordinates and
the unwrapped fibre coordinate. The renderer's geodesics and distance
calculation account for the coupling.

```{r sl2r, fig.alt="Three intrinsic balls in the universal cover of SL(2, R)."}
inside("sl2r")
```

## Moving and turning the observer

Set the observer location and orientation on `backend_3d()`. The columns of
`facing` are the right, up and forward unit tangent vectors in the observer's
orthonormal frame. The example below moves sideways in Nil and turns by five
degrees. The backend's field of view controls the full-panel perspective
image; the exterior camera's azimuth and elevation do not set this view.

```{r moved, fig.alt="Nil scene viewed from an observer moved sideways and turned five degrees."}
angle <- 5 * pi / 180
facing <- matrix(c(cos(angle), 0, -sin(angle), 0, 1, 0,
  sin(angle), 0, cos(angle)), 3, 3)
inside("nil") + coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raymarch", geometry = "nil",
  observer = c(0.05, 0, 0), facing = facing, fov = 90,
  dpi = 52, antialias = 1, max_distance = 3.5, max_steps = 256))
```

The light is located at the observer. Its diffuse intensity depends on the
area density of geodesic spheres along the viewing ray. Use the ambient and
diffuse strengths of `light_3d()` to adjust illumination. The maximum ray
length and step count bound the rendering work; small distant objects may
need a longer range or more steps.

## Following a ray numerically

The same geodesic kernel is available for numerical inspection. Its result
contains positions, orthonormal-frame velocities, coordinate velocities,
parallel-transport matrices and area densities. For a Euclidean ray the area
density grows as squared distance; the following output compares it with the
spherical and hyperbolic cases.

```{r ray-area}
distances <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5)
areas <- data.frame(distance = distances,
  Euclidean = geodesic_3d("e3", distance = distances)$area,
  Spherical = geodesic_3d("s3", distance = distances)$area,
  Hyperbolic = geodesic_3d("h3", distance = distances)$area)
knitr::kable(areas, digits = 3)
```

## Identifying domain faces

A quotient identifies boundary faces of a fundamental domain, the region
used to represent the space. A ray crossing one face continues through its
paired face with its tangent transported by the pairing isometry. This
Euclidean example identifies the two x faces by translations of two units.

```{r portals}
to_left <- to_right <- diag(4)
to_left[1, 4] <- -2
to_right[1, 4] <- 2
faces <- list(
  thurston_portal_3d(c(1, 0, 0, 0), 1, to_left),
  thurston_portal_3d(c(-1, 0, 0, 0), 1, to_right))
```

Place a ball beyond the right-facing boundary in the identified space.
Repeated copies become visible along rays that cross the domain faces.
For other geometries, supply isometries in the embeddings documented by
`thurston_portal_3d()` and every paired face of the intended domain.

```{r quotient, fig.alt="Repeated views of an orange ball in a Euclidean domain periodic along x."}
ggplot() + geom_thurston_3d(center = c(-0.5, 0, 1.5), radius = 0.3,
  fill = PAL["orange"]) + theme_void() +
  coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raymarch", quotient = faces,
    fov = 110, max_distance = 5, dpi = 52, antialias = 1))
```
